prize_parts.citation: for the development of optical lattice clocks reaching a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18, opening new regimes of precision measurement

statement.case_for: I keep B024 first after reading the colleagues' ballots. Optical lattice clocks are the clearest advance on the shortlist in what can be measured and how accurately: the magic-wavelength idea removes the light-shift problem that previously limited many-atom interrogation, and the resulting 10^-18 uncertainties are now confirmed by independent clocks in several countries and compared across continents. The consequences are concrete rather than promissory: relativistic geodesy at the centimetre level, tighter limits on drifting fundamental constants and dark-matter couplings, and the leading route to a redefinition of the second. The credit is also unusually clean for this list: Katori proposed the lattice scheme and demonstrated the early clocks, and Ye's group drove strontium to record accuracy and stability, so a two-person prize is natural and leaves no obvious omitted principal among the credited names. Lindroth and Olsson also rank it in their top three, which suggests the case is legible to colleagues outside my own subfield, not just to atomic physicists.
statement.case_against: The strongest counterargument is one of novelty relative to earlier precision-spectroscopy prizes: 2005 recognised laser-based precision spectroscopy and the optical frequency comb, and 2012 recognised control of single quantum systems including ion clocks, so a sceptical member can read lattice clocks as the next increment on an already honoured line. A second reservation, which I take seriously, is that the clock community is wider than two names: Ludlow, Lemonde, Ovsiannikov, Takamoto and others made decisive contributions to the accuracy milestones, and the history of who first demonstrated which step is partly recalled rather than verified here. Finally, the headline fundamental-physics payoff (a new-physics detection or a formal redefinition of the second) has not yet arrived, so some colleagues will weigh B024 as a measurement achievement rather than a discovery.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene (B021) first, arguing that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the correlated-insulator and superconducting observations is a clean theory-to-experiment chain with timely recognition and high breadth.
responses.response: I agree that the prediction-plus-discovery structure is cleaner than most, and that B021 deserves to be a serious finalist. Where I differ is on maturity: the 2018 results are only eight years old and, as Eriksson himself notes, the origin of the superconductivity is still debated, so what would be honoured is a phenomenon whose interpretation is not settled. Lattice clocks have a decade-plus record of independent confirmation with a stable physical picture. I would not call B021 wrong, only less secure on timing. I also note the credit boundary around Yuan Cao and the other experimental groups, which Mehlig and Pearce also flag, is more open here than for the clocks.

responses.point: Mehlig places B021 first for the simple, tunable idea (twist angle controls interaction strength) and values the combination of a sharp theoretical prediction and broad downstream impact, while acknowledging an interval of only about eight years since the discovery.
responses.response: The conceptual economy of the twist-angle idea is real, and I would not dispute its originality. My disagreement is that breadth of follow-on activity is not the same as settled understanding; a literature that is still growing rapidly partly reflects open questions. Mehlig's own maturity note concedes the pairing mechanism is unresolved. If the committee decides to reward the field before its interpretation stabilises, I could support B021 as my alternative, but I would then want the citation to be framed on the flat-band prediction and the observation of correlated states and not on superconductivity.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, ranks the topological insulator candidate B030 first as one of the strongest cases for lasting impact, with a stable interpretation after more than fifteen years, and ranks B024 only sixth.
responses.response: I accept that B030 is mature and conceptually important, and the 15-year confirmation record is a genuine strength. My reservation is overlap with the 2016 prize on topological phases of matter, which several colleagues (Lindroth, Mehlig, Johansson) also raise, and the three-person limit forces a hard choice among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang authors, which I regard as a more difficult attribution problem than the clock pair. I would ask Pearce why B024 sits as low as sixth: is the concern the proximity to 2005 and 2012, or the perceived lack of a discovery in the narrow sense? I think the answer matters, because I see the clocks as distinct from the comb itself.

responses.point: Lindroth also ranks optical lattice clocks first, finding the magic-wavelength and light-shift physics convincing, and she notes that independent clocks in several countries confirm the performance.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific assessment and with her point that this invention is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. One qualification I would add to her note on credit: the two-name credit is clean among the listed names, but the committee should be explicit that Ludlow, Lemonde and others on the accuracy side are being passed over, and the citation should be written around the lattice-clock scheme and its 10^-18 realisation rather than around the strontium system alone.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B002) first and trapped ions (B006) second, arguing that circuit QED is the architecture of essentially every superconducting processor, while noting that the timing relative to the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits needs weighing.
responses.response: The impact of circuit QED on quantum technology is undeniable, but the very recent 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, which Johansson himself raises, makes the same platform a risky choice so soon, and the four-name credit forces a choice between theory and experiment. On trapped ions (B006) I am closer to him: the Cirac-Zoller proposal and Blatt's experiments are foundational, and I list B006 as an alternative, though the overlap with Wineland's 2012 prize applies there with greater force than it does for lattice clocks.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 (frequency combs) and 2012 (single-quantum-system control) prizes, which is the main factor that could lower B024.
The finer history of who first demonstrated the magic-wavelength lattice clock and who first reached 10^-18 is recalled from memory and not verified against primary sources in this stage.
Whether the committee prefers a measurement-capability prize now, or waits for a fundamental-physics result such as a redefinition of the second or a new-physics limit.
If B021 gains broad support, how much weight to give to the unsettled superconducting mechanism relative to the robustness of the correlated-insulator phenomenology.
statement.conflict_note: No direct conflict with the credited names is apparent from my profile. I note two indirect connections for transparency: I spent time in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my doctoral period, and Hall's group and the frequency-comb tradition sit in the intellectual background of precision optical clocks; and as a Lund atomic physicist with a background in laser spectroscopy I work in a neighbouring field. I have no documented collaboration or supervisory relationship with Katori or Ye, and the Lund colleagues listed in my profile (Svanberg, Aldén, Rippe, Walther, Kinos) and my WACQT and Deep Light Vision roles do not concern any shortlisted candidate. The committee may wish to note the Hall connection when weighing my ranking of B024.
